t20: The secret to a good house party isn't the budget or the venue,
t22: . The same people, in the same house, with the same music, can make one night unforgettable or have everyone gone by 11 PM. The difference is what you do and when you do it.
t24: A house party naturally divides into three, and each part has its job. If you plan with this in mind, the "what should we do now" gap never appears.
t26: Not everyone has arrived yet, the mood is calm. Music in the background, conversation up front. Don't start a game.
t28: The group is complete, energy is high. This is where games belong.
t30: Pace drops. Games end, music gets quieter, conversation resumes.
t31: Prep: things to do before the party
t33: Choosing songs as the night goes is the most time-wasting thing.
t34: Put all snacks in one place.
t35: A scattered table sends people to the kitchen and breaks up the group.
t36: Arrange seating close to a circle.
t37: A setup where everyone sees each other makes games naturally possible.
t39: A game that isn't asked for doesn't get played; keep it open on your phone.
t41: Not having something separate for non-drinking guests is the most common mistake of the night.
t43: The most common mistake is starting too early. A game started before the group is warmed up falls flat and gets the label "this game didn't work"; but the problem isn't the game, it's the timing.
t44: The right moment is when everyone has arrived and the first round of conversation naturally winds down — usually 45–60 minutes after the start. That moment of quiet is perfect for a game.
t45: What do you play in order?
t47: Vote-based, doesn't put anyone on the spot. Like "who most..."
t49: Spinner or task-based; the highest-energy part of the night.
t51: Two teams, word guessing. Competition bonds the group.
t53: A calm guessing game or chat mode.

t55: A game with a long rule explanation
t56: A crowd waiting for their turn — prefer modes where everyone plays at once
t57: One person constantly changing the music
t58: Insisting on a game nobody wants to play
t59: Pressuring a guest who doesn't want to drink — have an alcohol-free alternative always at the table
t61: This content is for 18+ readers. In games played with alcohol, never pressure anyone to drink, define an alcohol-free penalty option upfront, keep water and food on the table. For guests who will drive, the alcohol-free version is always a valid choice.
t62: Leaving the game side to the app
t63: Shot Spinner brings the player list, weighted spinner, five difficulty levels, and a live scoreboard to one screen. Open it mid-party and start spinning — it works with 2 to 12 players and can be played in an alcohol-free setup too.
t65: When should games start at a house party?
t66: After everyone arrives and the first conversation round naturally winds down — usually 45–60 minutes after the start. Starting too early makes games fall flat.
t67: How many games should you play?
t68: Three or four modes, 60–70 minutes total, is ideal. Changing modes keeps the group's energy up better than stretching one game.
t69: What about guests who don't drink?
t70: Define the alcohol-free version of the game upfront: use point loss or double task as penalties. Never pressure anyone to drink; have water and non-alcoholic drinks at the table.
t72: Spin the spinner, take a task by difficulty level, earn points or take a shot.
